title: Mencius's Mother Moves House Three Times
text:
Mencius, the great Confucian thinker of the fourth century BC, lost his father when he was small and was raised by his mother. Liu Xiang, a scholar of the Han dynasty, collected her story in his Biographies of Exemplary Women.

At first they lived near a cemetery. The boy played at funerals, digging and wailing like the mourners. His mother decided this was no place to raise a son and moved near a market. Now he played at buying and selling, imitating the hawkers' cries. She moved again, this time next to a school. There the boy began to imitate the rituals of the students and teachers, bowing, yielding and practicing ceremony. His mother said that this was a place fit for her son, and they stayed.

Mencius grew up to become, in later Chinese memory, the second sage after Confucius. "Mencius's mother moved three times" became a Chinese proverb for the care a parent takes over a child's surroundings.
lesson: Children absorb their surroundings long before they absorb our advice. Choosing where and among whom they grow up may be one of the most important things a parent decides.
source: Liu Xiang, Lienu Zhuan (Biographies of Exemplary Women), Book 1, The Mother of Meng Ke
caveat: The story was written down about three centuries after Mencius lived and is best read as tradition.
